title: Streaming signal-loss analysis and runbook draft
content:
Executive summary:

- Incident type: P0 streaming session degradations causing partial signal loss (clients saw stalled chunks, reconnects, and high 5xx for streamed responses).
- Window: 2026-10-27 22:13 UTC -> 2026-10-27 23:37 UTC (84 minutes).
- Impact: ~18% of streaming sessions in us-west experienced prolonged stalls or reconnects; non-streaming (non-HTTP chunked) traffic largely unaffected. Several high-value tenant integrations reported degraded UX.
- Brief cause hypothesis: Interplay between the adaptive request coalescer (edge batching/autocoalesce) and concurrent KV-cache lease eviction logic created a transient lock/starvation pattern on streaming workers, causing long tail serialization and partial request timeouts.

The symptom cluster we observed:

- Surge of streaming write stalls with socket idle timers touching 30–90s before client reconnects.
- Elevated 5xx rates on streaming endpoints concurrent with high write latency (server-side ts store showed heavy write queue depth).
- Edge proxy logs show many connections entering STREAMING-WAIT state, followed by repeated STALL/RETRY events.
- KV cache metrics: increased lease churn and repeated preemptive evictions in the same key prefix ranges.

High-level timeline (local on-call synthesis):

- 22:10 UTC — Small uptick in streaming session concurrency in us-west (normal customer traffic pattern + weekly batch).
- 22:13 UTC — First Pager triggered: streaming write-latency SLO alert (p0_stream_write_p99 > 1.5s).
- 22:20 UTC — SRE on-call (Samira) investigates; identifies correlation with KV-cache eviction spikes and dispatcher queue growth.
- 22:28 UTC — Engineering paged; mitigations attempted: temporarily increasing KV lease TTL in us-west to reduce churn (quick config flip).
- 22:35 UTC — Partial improvement; stalls still present for long-tail sessions. Evidence points to scheduler coalescing causing head-of-line blocking.
- 22:50 UTC — Hotfix deployed to edge: disable adaptive coalescing for streaming routes in us-west (config flag).
- 23:02 UTC — Streaming metrics start trending down; reconnect rate normalizes.
- 23:37 UTC — Incident declared resolved; retrospective notes collected.

What we changed during the event (short-term mitigations):

1) Increased KV lease TTL for us-west cache cluster (reduced eviction frequency).
2) Temporarily disabled adaptive coalescing / aggressive batch merging for streaming endpoints.
3) Applied a conservative rate-shedding rule for very large session prefixes to prevent single-prefix hotspots from dominating worker threads.
4) Raised streaming write-queue warning threshold to trigger alerts earlier.

Why those mitigations were chosen:

- Increasing KV lease TTL reduced churn quickly without code changes (config-level rollbackable).
- Disabling coalescing removed a source of head-of-line blocking where a merged large batch would stall worker processing for many smaller streaming sessions.
- Rate-shedding buys time during storms by preventing single prefix walks from saturating pool; conservative and reversible.

Root cause analysis (current working theory):

- Trigger: A normal weekly batch increased concurrency on a small subset of prefixes (observed heavy skew).
- Amplifier A: Adaptive coalescing merged heterogeneous streaming requests into larger batches to improve throughput. When a large/slow input entered the batch (long generation or a backend stall), the whole batch waited, causing worker stalls for other streaming sessions in that batch.
- Amplifier B: KV-cache eviction/lease-reacquisition code incurred short synchronous locks when a prefix eviction occurred under high contention. These locks amplified head-of-line blocking by preventing other coroutines from progressing while they waited for lease handoff.
- Net result: Combined scheduler-level coalescing and the synchronous eviction path created a cascade — once a few large batches stalled, many streaming workers queued, causing socket timeouts and eventual client reconnects (5xxs).

Evidence supporting the RCA:

- Traces: span traces show long blocking periods inside dispatcher::coalesce_and_dispatch and kvcache::evict_sync between 22:12–22:35 UTC.
- Metrics: worker_active_count climbs and worker_queue_depth p99 spikes concurrent with kv_lease_operations_rate.
- Repro: Local load test using a small number of hot prefixes with batchable streaming requests reproduced the stall when both coalescing and eviction rates were high. Disabling coalescing eliminated the stall in the test harness.

Open/uncertain areas:

- Why did eviction churn spike so quickly for those prefixes? Hypothesis: client retry pattern + small TTL combined to continually refresh lease ownership under contention. Need to correlate client SDK behaviours.
- Is there an off-by-one or lock contention in lease handoff code that makes eviction path synchronous for unrelated keys?
- Long-term interaction between coalescing heuristics and tail-latency-sensitive workloads needs quantification.

Immediate followups (action items - owner and ETA):

- SRE: Stabilize runbook and add playbook steps for this pattern (Samira) — ETA 2026-11-10.
- Serving-runtime: Convert synchronous eviction path to async handoff; add metrics for eviction lock hold duration (Evan) — ETA RFC 2026-12-05, PR by 2027-01-15.
- Serving-runtime: Add a coalescing safety net for streaming routes (max batch timeout and per-prefix concurrency cap) (Priya) — ETA 2026-12-01.
- SDK: Investigate client retry behavior that may exacerbate prefix churn (Noah) — ETA 2026-11-20.
- Observability: Create a composite alert that surfaces co-occurrence of kv_lease_eviction_rate > X and streaming_write_p99 > Y (Samira/Evan) — ETA 2026-11-05.
- Postmortem write-up: Formal postmortem to be drafted with timeline + RCA + followups (Samira) — ETA 2026-11-12.

Runbook draft (quick steps for on-call) — initial version:

1) Detection
  - Alert: streaming_write_p99 > 1.5s for >5min in a region OR streaming_reconnect_rate > 2x baseline for >3min.
  - Secondary signals: kv_lease_eviction_rate > baseline and worker_queue_depth p99 rising.

2) Triage
  - Identify affected region and serving fleet (region tag + model route).
  - Check span traces for dispatcher::coalesce_and_dispatch and kvcache::evict_sync.
  - Run small query: top 10 prefixes by request rate in the last 5 minutes.

3) Quick mitigations (order matters)
  - A) Increase KV lease TTL (config flip scoped to region) to reduce churn.
  - B) Disable adaptive coalescing for streaming routes (flags: streaming.coalesce.enabled=false) to remove head-of-line risk.
  - C) Apply temporary per-prefix concurrency cap (config) if a single prefix > 40% of streaming sessions.
  - D) If stalls persist, redirect new streaming sessions to a fallback router (fallback config that serves with coalescing off).

4) Communications
  - Update #sre-status and the incidents channel with mitigation steps and ETA.
  - Coordinate CS for affected high-value tenants (include mitigation details and ETA).

5) Recovery verification
  - Confirm streaming_write_p99 back within SLO and reconnect rate normalized for 15 minutes.
  - Roll back temporary changes in reverse order after stabilization (C, B, A).

6) Post-incident tasks
  - Attach traces + sample request ids to the Jira ticket.
  - Run the localized load test that reproduces the degredation and validate code changes in staging.

Monitoring and instrumentation changes proposed:

- Emit eviction_lock_hold_ms histogram and alert when p99 > 100ms.
- Add a coalescer_batch_size_by_route metric with percentiles to detect large batches forming on streaming routes.
- Create a composite alert rule that combines kv_lease_eviction_rate and streaming_write_p99 to surface the combined failure mode earlier.

Customer notes / communications (draft snippet for CS):

- Short summary: On 2026-10-27 we observed a regional streaming disruption that caused intermittent stalls and reconnects for some streaming integrations. We implemented configuration mitigations that restored normal service and are working on a permanent fix.
- What we did: temporarily disabled an adaptive batching optimization for streaming routes and adjusted cache lease settings to reduce eviction churn.
- What we’ll do: code changes to make eviction handoffs asynchronous and add safety limits to the coalescer so one slow request cannot stall many streaming clients.

Notes to self (on-call reflections):

- This felt like a systems-interaction bug — each individual subsystem behaved within design, but together they created a fragile operational point. More focus on cross-component integration tests needed.
- The runbook flow order mattered; we should codify the exact sequence (TTL -> coalescer off -> prefix cap) into an automated playbook.
- Consider periodic chaos tests that induce eviction churn + batch coalescing to validate tail-latency behavior before shipping heuristics.

Appendix (evidence pointers):

- Trace ids: span-samples attached to Jira ticket JIRA-SRE-8893.
- Metrics dashboards: streaming/us-west/write-latency, kvcache/us-west/lease-ops, worker/queue-depth.
- Repro harness: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sre-loadtests/tree/main/hot-prefix-streaming

End of draft.

Unresolved: Please annotate if you saw different evidence (especially SDK-related retry fingerprints). Add any alternative mitigation suggestions that are low-risk and reversible.
